In our investigation, we examined a comprehensive range of coding tasks including function completion, code translation, code summarization, code debugging, code pairwise evaluation, code generation with constraints and code generation with code-prompting. However, these studies frequently overlook that global minima are often set extremely small, creating inherent measurement difficulties. High-Performance Computing (HPC) system design, where the ability to recover from node failures while sustaining ongoing tasks is essential for achieving optimal availability. Contemporary Volatile Memory- based main systems store data primarily as in-page partial updates known as shadowing rather than relying on copy-on-write schemes to save space and boost performance, yet these implementations lack fault resilience, as failure during an update results in corrupted partial pages. This study introduces RVW (Reliable Virtual Memory Write), a novel, full-page, in-page partial update with fault tolerance integrated directly into the x86 virtual memory management framework. User space applications can specify the granularity of their memory writes to balance space usage, the rate of changes, and system robustness. To manage potential corruption, RVW employs redundancy across multiple pages and utilizes existing copy-on-write mechanisms for page allocation. The system achieves full recovery with just one redundant copy, requiring only a minor performance penalty even in failure scenarios. Benchmarking on a state-of-the-art supercomputer shows RVD delivers main system availability exceeding 99.99%, a survival rate of over 97% against single component failures, and an average 14.1% lower memory usage compared to current copy-on-write systems.
